newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - S.Africa budget at half-year - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - S.Africa budget at half-year - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd
According to the Ministry of Finance the budget at the half-way stage seems to be on track to reach the estimated budget deficit of 5.1 percent of estimated GDP.
Issues from the exchequer have so far amounted to 49.2 percent of the total budgeted amount for 1996/97. However, this does not include issues from amounts brought forward from previous years.

The receipts are lagging slightly at 48.7 percent, but then receipts are normally lower in the first half of the year, and there is also clear evidence of an acceleration of receipts in the last quarter.

The receipts to date, however, include a substantial one-off capital receipt of 1.9 billion rand from the sale of oil reserves. Excluding this, the ordinary revenue into the exchequer so far amounts to 47.4 percent of the budget estimate, but the full projected estimate still appears attainable.
At this stage one has to give the Receiver of Revenue the benefit of the doubt with regard to his claim of being able to find another 1.5 billion rand from improvements in collections.

The expenditure figure is deceptively on track at 49.2 percent. Of the 85.5 billion rand requisitions for the first six months 17.0 billion rand was in respect of interest payments and this is 50.5 percent of the estimate for the year. The non-interest expenditure turns out to be 48.9 percent of budget.

This is still not too badly off target. The shortfall, nevertheless, is presumably reflective of the inability of departments to spend on development projects for organisational reasons. The same reason could account for the relatively low expenditure of only 363 million rand from rolled over funds, reportedly in excess of five billion rand.
What was a most vexing problem of a lack of control of government expenditures because of the practise of rolling over funds could well fall away because of government inertia.
In effect then the budget may be said to be on track because of the departmental inability to perform compensating for the overrun on interest payments.

The interest overrun in the first half may at first glance appear to be not too bad. However, it has to be borne in mind that the interest bill must always be significantly greater in the second half when interest payments on borrowings in the first half fall due in addition to the interest bill on outstanding debt.

In the last few years the interest bill in the first half has averaged 47.2 percent of the full year's bill. On this basis then the overrun of interest for the first half of this year will have been as much as 1.1 billion rand.

The overrun on interest in the first half will have arisen in respect of higher than expected discount rates on short-term Treasury bills and other short-term funding instruments. Market rates have remained higher than expected basically because of balance of payments reasons.

Too often the calculations of interest turn out to be the Achilles heel of budgeting, despite the great care put into the exercise. In this case the underassessment has arisen from the roseate view taken of financial markets at the time of making estimates.

There are reasons to suppose this was in January when the yield on the ten-year bond, the R150, was running below 14 percent. The market turned bearish soon after and throughout the 1996/97 budget year to date the yields have been between 15.0 percent and 16.5 percent, but below 15.0 percent for a short spell.

A number of reasons may be given for the market turning bearish, such as the foreign investor in general preferring equities instead of bonds on the JSE because of the rand collapse, domestic institutions shifting into equities in the packages designed for asset swaps, the taxation of pension fund interest income, government pension funds no longer being captive buyers of government stock, and the facility of the zero-interest bonds which are proving to be a two-edged sword.
In short government has been working hard at reducing the pool of loanable funds it may draw from in financing the budget deficit - and paying for it by having to issue more paper at a higher cost.

The budget as presented in March projected an overall borrowing requirement of 45.1 billion rand to meet a deficit of 28.8 billion rand and the redemption of past loans amounting to 16.3 billion rand.

Net short-term loans of three billion rand and foreign loans of 2.5 billion rand were provided for, leaving 39.6 billion rand to be found on a cash flow basis through the issue of local government stock.

However, the markets seemed so encouraging at the time of preparing the estimates that only a discount on stock issued of 2.8 billion rand was allowed, giving an overall face value of stock to be issued 42.4 billion rand.
In the event the accumulated discount on local registered stock in these first six months has been 4.0 billion rand.

The nominal amount of interest bearing stock issued in the half year was 22.5 billion rand; but this only yielded a cash flow into the exchequer of 18.5 billion rand. But, there was, in addition, a gross issue of long dated zero-interest stock of 881 million rand. A total nominal value of stock of 23.4 billion rand has thus been raised, which will lift the interest bill by approximately 1.8 billion rand in a full year, but some 300 million rand more than originally projected in a full year and 150 million rand in the second half of 1996/97.
Government would appear to be on track to having to pay an extra 2.4 billion rand on its interest bill.
However, there will also be a substantial extra cost on what the Ministry of Finance describes as Management costs on state debt.
This just happens to be the difference in rand terms between the current redemption value of foreign loans to be redeemed in October, December and next February and their original book value.
This was first estimated in January before the collapse of the rand at 858 million rand, but at current exchange rates will amount to 1,135 million rand, or some extra 280 million rand.
The upshot of all this is that should revenues and non-interest expenditures turn out to be as originally estimated the budget deficit will be 31.45 billion rand, or 5.6 percent of GDP.

However, with the distinct likelihood of departments continuing to underperform on development expenditures the final outturn will be somewhat better with the deficit lying between 5.1 percent and 5.6 percent of GDP.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
